newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs make new threat to Bosnian local elections.
newsitem.headline: Serbs make new threat to Bosnian local elections.

text.p: The Bosnian Serbs on Friday cast further doubt on their participation in local elections scheduled for next month, saying conditions for the politically sensitive polls were becoming "almost impossible".
Hardline Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic used a crisis surrounding the resettlement of Moslems in villages in Serb held territory to erect further obstacles to taking part in the elections.

She was speaking after talks with Robert Frowick of the United States, head of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe mission to Bosnia, the body charged with supervising the elections due on November 23 and 24.
Frowick, who has tried to persuade the Serbs to accept OSCE supervision of the municipal polls, said nothing to reporters.
Plavsic accused the Moslems, being resettled under agreement with the international community, of entering Bosnian Serb territory "forcibly".
"The situation is getting more complicated by the hour and conditions for local elections are getting to be almost impossible," she said in the northern town of Banja Luka.
"If the process of forcible settlement in this manner continues, then we cannot say that conditions for local elections are being created."

The resettlement of Moslem villagers in Bosnian Serb areas of northern Bosnia has been accompanied by the blowing up of a number of houses. United Nations officials have pointed the finger at the Serbs.
But at the same time, the Moslems have been found to have arms and ammunition in their houses and three were arrested and later released by Serb police on Friday.
Plavsic's statement was a renewed blow to the OSCE, already under fire for its handling of elections on September 14 for a Bosnia's multiethnic governing bodies.

In a letter to Frowick on Monday she said that since the Serbs had their own parliament, there was no reason why they should not call their own local elections with their own rules and without OSCE supervision.
Plavsic's stance came despite clear warnings from the West that the Bosnian Serbs risk losing their share of reconstruction funds if they did not play their part in the political process.

British Foreign Office minister Sir Nicholas Bonsor, who met Plavsic earlier on Friday, told her: "I believe when the structure of government is in place the international community will be in a much better position to help financially in terms of encouraging investment in your country."
The Serbs infuriated the international community last Saturday by boycotting the inaugural session of Bosnia's newly elected parliament and presidency.

Serb media meanwhile said officials of the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development had used a visit to the Bosnian Serb headquarters at Pale to impose new conditions on post-war investment aid.
Bosnian Serb Prime Minister Gojko Klickovic said he would not give in to "blackmail" even if he needed the money.
